title: I Posted the Community Smokehouse Rack Hours After They Took My Numbered Brisket

parts.text: I opened the smokehouse at 6:08 a.m. and chair Pitt was already hanging on my numbered rack. The slate said: ONE RACK. EIGHT HOURS. MEAT STAYS WITH THE BOOKING. I was forty-three, co-op cook, holding a probe ticket that listed our cook. Pitt shrugged. "Chairs are the smoke." I photographed the slate, the booking, and his brisket on my hooks. Then I asked for the rack log. At 6:16 the yard pinged why Pitt's name was on my rack. I kept my voice yard-quiet and let the timestamp talk. A slate is only a slate until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The yard can see Pitt's brisket on my hooks during our booking.

social.video_title: He hung on my numbered rack with my brisket — Part 1/2
social.description: Smokehouse, a chair on my hooks, an eight-hour slate he posted. I logged the brisket. Would you have asked for the rack log?

parts.text: Pitt called it overflow until the yard asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the slate, and the brisket still. The rack went back to my hooks. Pitt ran his own eight and told the next chair atmosphere was always about bark. Bark is a word chairs use when a booking exists. Rack policy now has a second line: CHAIRS ARE NOT THE SMOKE. I keep our probe on a labeled clip. Pitt brown-bags his jokes. The yard finally looks like a booking, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.video_title: Chairs are not the smoke — Part 2/2
social.description: Rack log, numbered hooks, and a second line on the slate. Was overflow ever my brisket?
